title: ACLU blasts Trump’s new orders on birthright citizenship, saying they are doomed to fail in court– live
summary: President’s orders come month after supreme court struck down administration’s earlier attempt to place restrictions on birthright citizenship enshrined in US constitution
body: Despite an endorsement from Donald Trump on Thursday, congressman Andy Ogles, a far-right Tennessee Republican, seems to be in danger of losing his re-election bid to a primary challenger backed by the state’s governor, Bill Lee,. With nearly two-thirds of the votes counted in the party’s primary on Thursday night, Ogles trails Charlie Hatcher, a former state commissioner of agriculture, by more than 5 points, according to a running tally from the Associated Press. “Congressman Andy Ogles is doing a fantastic job representing the incredible people of Tennessee’s 5th Congressional District!” Trump wrote on his social media platform as Tennessee Republicans went to the polls on Thursday. “Andy Ogles my Complete and Total Endorsement for Re-Election. Election Day for the Republican Primary is TODAY. GET OUT AND VOTE FOR ANDY”. An Ogles defeat would be the second loss of a Trump-backed candidate in a Republican primary this week. The executive orders signed on Thursday by Donald Trump, in which he tries, again, to undermine the guarantee of birthright citizenship enshrined in the US constitution reaffirmed by the supreme court just five weeks ago, is part of a quixotic campaign he has waged for more than a decade. At a Republican presidential primary campaign event in Orlando, Florida in November 2015, Trump hinted that he had a plan to end what he called the scourge of “anchor babies”, a derogatory term for children of undocumented immigrants born in the United States as citizens. “You can’t come into the country- you’re illegal, you come down, you sit down, you have your baby, and we take care of the baby for the next 85 years!” Trump said. “Everybody says, ‘Well, you need a constitutional amendment; it’ll take 15 years; it’ll never happen’. You don’t, you don’t. You need a simple act of Congress. You might not even need that.” If elected, Trump promised the crowd at a resort near Disney World, “the anchor baby, birthright citizenship, it’s over, not going to happen.” Three years later, as president, Trump said in a televised interview with Jonathan Swan just before the 2018 midterms that he planned to issue an executive order to instruct federal agencies that children born in the United States to non-citizens were not entitled to US citizenship at birth. “It was always told to me that you needed a constitutional amendment. Guess what? You don’t,” Trump told Swan in an interview excerpt posted online on 30 October 2018. “You can definitely do it with an act of Congress,” Trump added, incorrectly, “but now they’re saying I can do it just with an executive order.” As Swan reported at the time, Trump’s claim that he could undo the birthright citizenship guaranteed by the 14th Amendment to the constitution was a minority view among legal scholars, but was supported by a then-obscure figure: John Eastman, who had argued for decades that the amendment granting citizenship to “All persons born or naturalized in the United States, and subject to the jurisdiction thereof,” should be read to exclude the children of people who are not US citizens when their child is born. Eastman later claimed in a 2020 Newsweek op-ed that Kamala Harris was ineligible for the vice-presidency because she had no right to US citizenship at birth, since she was born in Oakland, California in 1964 to non-citizen parents who were, “subject to the jurisdiction” of their native lands of India and Jamaica. In the 2018 interview, Trump called birthright citizenship “ridiculous,” and falsely asserted that the US is “the only country in the world where a person comes in and has a baby, and the baby is essentially a citizen.” In fact, at least 30 nations grant citizenship this way. He also claimed that an executive order was in the process of being drafted. Although that order did not materialize until the start of Trump’s second term, his obsession with casting doubt on the citizenship of children born in the US to foreign parents has had a clearly political element from the start. After all, Trump’s original rise to political prominence was tied to his false claim that Barack Obama, born to an American mother and a Kenyan father in Honolulu, just two years after Hawaii became a state, might have been born outside the US. Then, after Joe Biden picked Harris as his running mate in 2020, Trump repeatedly refused to confirm that she was eligible for an elected office open only to “a natural born Citizen.” Instead, Trump called the question Eastman raised about Harris’s citizenship at birth in his Newsweek op-ed “very serious” and a potential “problem” for her. He also praised Eastman as “a very highly qualified, very talented lawyer” and called him “brilliant”. Eastman, who went on to devise the fake electors scheme designed to keep Trump in office after he lost the 2020 election, and gave an inflammatory speech before the Capitol riot on January 6 2021, was finally disbarred by the California supreme court in April, based on “clear and convincing evidence that he advanced false claims about the 2020 presidential election to mislead courts, public officials, and the American public.” The American Civil Liberties Union is not impressed by the legal reasoning of Donald Trump’s new executive orders in which he is once again attempting to restrict birthright citizenship, just five weeks after the US supreme court struck a similar order he issued last year. In a statement, the ACLU blasted the president’s attempted end-run around the supreme court decision and predicted that the new orders will not survive a court challenge. “The Supreme Court already decided this issue: Birthright citizenship is guaranteed by the Constitution. No additional executive order can change the meaning of the Constitution,” the deputy director of the ACLU’s Immigrants’ Rights Project, Cody Wofsy, said. “Any executive order that tries to rewrite birthright citizenship will meet the same fate as the last one”. Speaking to reporters on Thursday, Donald Trump refused to confirm a Washington Post report that he told donors at a recent Oval Office meeting that they need to help his vice-president, JD Vance, win the 2028 presidential election. “At the end of the day, we need to elect JD,” Trump reportedly told the donors two weeks ago, the Post reported. “Mr President,” a reporter asked, “there is a report that you told donors that they need to get JD Vance elected in 2028. Is that your official endorsement?” “No,” Trump answered. “I heard about it a little while ago,” Trump continued, apparently referring to the report published on Thursday. “I think he’s great, but we’re way too early to even be thinking about that.” The two new executive orders on birthright citizenship signed by Donald Trump on Thursday, just five weeks ago after the US supreme court struck down his previous order denying citizenship to the children of non-citizens, attempt to limit in two ways a right that has been enshrined in the constitution since the 14th amendment was ratified in 1868. One order bars the entry of foreigners allegedly traveling to the US “for the purpose of giving birth on American soil”, without saying how, exactly, that determination is to be made. (It might be worth noting here that such a policy, had it been in effect in 2001, might well have prevented Folarin Balogun, who was born that year to a mother visiting New York from London, from being born a US citizen and going on to represent the US in this summer’s World Cup.) The second order seeks to deny citizenship to the children of certain categories of non-citizens. The order excludes children born to any non-citizen parent in the following categories: an alien enemy, “defined to include any member of a designated Foreign Terrorist Organization … or Specially Designated Global Terrorist”; foreign government employees, including: ambassadors; other embassy or consulate employees who are nationals of that foreign country; anyone employed by a foreign government in an official capacity; employees of international organizations that possess international-organization immunity; people “engaged in a commercial transaction to purchase or access birthright citizenship”. The children of foreign ambassadors have long been excluded from birthright citizenship. Somewhat redundantly, the second order also denies citizenship to the children of non-citizens “born in a territory or territorial waters of the United States where citizenship is not conferred by Federal statute”. Speaking in the Oval Office earlier on Thursday, Donald Trump gave a wildly inaccurate account of the nature and timing of the 14th amendment to the US constitution, which enshrined the principle of birthright citizenship, as he sought to justify two new executive orders attempting to deny citizenship to a wider pool of children born on US soil to non-citizens. As he discussed the orders, “Continuing to Protect the Meaning and Value of American Citizenship” and “Ending Birth Tourism”, Trump called the supreme court’s decision to strike down his previous attempt to deny birthright citizenship through executive action “a very, very unfortunate decision.” “So we’re, making adjustments because it’s very unfair,” the president said. “This was meant for the babies of slaves. It was right after – one week or two weeks after – the Civil war ended.” In fact, General Robert E Lee surrendered the largest of the Confederate forces on 9 April 1865 at Appomattox Court House in Virginia. More than a year later, the 14th amendment was passed by Congress on 13 June 1866, and ratified on 9 July 9 1868. Trump’s assertion that the framers of the amendment only intended it to apply to the children of former slaves was roundly rejected by the supreme court, not this year but in 1898, when the justices ruled 6-2 that Wong Kim Ark, who was born in San Francisco to parents who were both Chinese citizens, was a US citizen by birth. Despite that well-known precedent, which was discussed at length during the r…

title: After decades of decline, New Zealand’s wool industry is making a comeback
summary: Forty years ago there were more than 22 sheep to every New Zealander, but wool prices and production declined with the uptake of synthetic alternatives
body: John Hargreaves’ family has farmed sheep and beef in Kaiwaka, north of Auckland, for generations. In the 1960s they had 3,000 ewes but in the decades since, as the value of wool declined and shearing costs grew, his flock slowly decreased to just over 1,700. But now, for the first time in roughly six years, his wool is making money. New Zealand’s once-famous wool industry is showing signs of a comeback, after the mounting costs of producing synthetic fabric triggered global demand for natural fibres. “We’re now covering our shearing costs and making some sort of a profit,” Hargreaves says. Sheep farming and wool production dominated New Zealand’s agricultural industry for nearly a century, with the number of sheep peaking at more than 70m by the 1980s – or roughly 22 sheep to every human. The economic policies of the 1980s, and a drop in global demand driven by the uptake of synthetic alternatives, drove down the price of wool. More recently, farmers have converted their pasture into more lucrative forestry blocks and dairy farming. There are now just over 23m sheep, or 4.5 sheep to every human, according to StatsNZ. But Dave Burridge, national wool auction manager for PGG Wrightson, says the tight supply of wool globally and rising oil prices driven by the Middle East conflict are pushing up demand for wool. “The raw material used to produce nylon and polyester fibres, they’ve all gone up in price,” pushing buyers from countries such as China and India towards natural fibres, he says. Major global brands are also seeking out New Zealand wool. In April, French luxury brand Chanel signed an investment deal with Central Otago’s Lammermoor Station, to part-own and support the production of premium wool. American outdoor clothing giant Patagonia visited New Zealand in June to eye up wool partnerships, and in May, Turkish carpet manufacturer Kalida Hali struck a deal with Wools of New Zealand. In June, the country’s wool fetched the highest prices in 15 years at the PGG Wrightson national auction – ranging from NZ$6.47 to NZ$6.80 a kilogram for crossbred fleeces, with top-quality, good-colour fleeces reaching nearly $8 a kilogram. There is still volatility in the market. Wool prices dipped at the most recent national auction, held in Christchurch on 30 July. The drop, partly driven by buyers stepping back after filling their commitments earlier in the season, was unsurprising, Burridge says. “There was always quiet concern by wool industry players that the price had gone up very quickly, like unparalleled rises that we’d never seen before, and … that things were going to probably come off at some stage.” But prices are still up $2 on a year ago and Burridge is optimistic for the industry’s future. “I feel really excited about the long-term prospects for wool, and convinced that wool will have its day in the sun again.” Federated Farmers’ wool and meat manager, Richard Dawkins, says the strong wool prices have buoyed farmers and there is cautious optimism for the future. “That continued awareness globally of sustainability and the attributes of wool – that is a positive outlook,” he says. Meanwhile, demand for New Zealand’s high-quality wool is increasing within India, New Zealand’s second-largest wool market, Dawkins says. A recent trade deal between the two countries will eliminate tariffs on wool, which is expected to strengthen exports. New Zealand’s culture now needs to re-embrace wool, to help bring stability to the market, Dawkins says. “This nation was built off the back of a sheep, built off wool … and that story’s been lost over the decades. It’s one thing asking the world to buy our product, but we need to embrace it ourselves as well.”

title: Trump signs new orders targeting birthright citizenship
summary: Orders come after supreme court rejected president’s first bid to restrict guarantee enshrined in US constitution
body: Donald Trump has made a second attempt to restrict the constitutional guarantee of birthright citizenship, just weeks after the US supreme court rejected his initial, more sweeping bid to deny automatic citizenship to the children born to undocumented immigrants and temporary foreign residents. Trump on Thursday signed two executive orders that seek to broaden the categories of children ineligible for automatic US citizenship and ban so-called “birth tourism”. The directives are expected to face legal challenges. Trump has long sought to dismantle birthright citizenship and has made the effort a centerpiece of his second-term immigration crackdown. He has thus far been unsuccessful. On Thursday, the president lashed out at the supreme court over what he called “a very unfortunate decision in the supreme court concerning birthright”. “It was close, but a very, very unfortunate decision,” Trump told reporters. “So we’re making adjustments because it’s very unfair.” A first new order seeks to expand the definitions of children who would not be able to receive birthright citizenship. Historical exceptions to the citizenship clause of the 14th amendment have included children born in the US to foreign sovereigns and diplomats; children of occupying foreign forces; children born on foreign ships; and children of Indigenous Americans. Stephen Miller, the White House deputy chief of staff and chief architect of Trump’s anti-immigration agenda, said the order aims to expand the categories to include children of members of “foreign terrorist organizations” as well as “large categories of people who lobby and act on behalf of foreign governments”, though it is unclear who would fall into the latter category. The order also seeks to broaden the exception of children born to foreign ambassadors to include more foreign government employees, and refers to people born in “a territory or territorial waters of the United States where citizenship is not conferred by federal statute” as ineligible. At the moment, that only includes American Samoa. The order would also deny birthright citizenship to children whose parents “engaged in fraudulent activity to obtain citizenship”. The second order targets “birth tourism” – travel to the US with the intention of giving birth so that the child will acquire US citizenship. Trump claimed on Thursday, without pointing at any evidence, that “hundreds of thousands” of people have undertaken this practice. “They’ve taken birthright citizenship and they’ve made a joke out of it,” Trump told reporters. “People are building businesses around it. That’s not the way it’s supposed ‌to work. It’s a disgrace. They’re buying their way in, and we’re not going to let it happen.” According to the Migration Policy Institute, the highest census-based estimate “puts birth tourism at 22,000 to 26,000 babies born annually on US soil, although government data show just 9,600 births to mothers with foreign addresses in 2024” – less than 1% of all the babies born in the United States each year. The second order directs federal agencies to target “birth tourism operators” who arrange such travel to the US. Traveling to the US under the guise of tourism while actually intending to give birth so the child automatically obtains citizenship constitutes visa fraud and is already illegal, raising questions about the practical implications of the new order beyond existing law. Thursday’s executive orders will almost certainly be challenged in court. On 30 June, the US supreme court voided his Day One-executive order denying automatic citizenship to children born to parents in the United States illegally or on temporary visas, reaffirming that the constitution guarantees citizenship to nearly everyone born on US soil are American citizens. Trump’s new directives aim to test the boundaries of that ruling by expanding the categories of people the administration argues fall outside the 14th amendment’s citizenship guarantee, while separately directing agencies to intensify their efforts to stop birth tourism. The American Civil Liberties Union on Thursday said the orders were another unconstitutional attempt to undo birthright citizenship after the administration’s defeat at the supreme court in June. “The supreme court already decided this issue: birthright citizenship is guaranteed by the constitution. No additional executive order can change the meaning of the constitution,” said Cody Wofsy, deputy director of the ACLU’s Immigrants’ Rights Project. “Any executive order that tries to rewrite birthright citizenship will meet the same fate as the last one.”

title: Typhoon Dim-sum: how Hong Kong put a tasty snack on the storm map
summary: A new name has been added to the list of future tropical cyclones for the Asia-Pacific region, including one with a culinary twist
body: A “Typhoon Dim-sum” could one day be on the horizon after the name was added to the Asia-Pacific region’s official list of tropical cyclone names this week. It features among nine names to be added to the list of future tropical cyclones, with each name contributed by a country. The names of tropical storms are generally recycled, replacing those which have caused serious casualties and economic loss. So how does a mouth-watering snack come to be endorsed by the UN-backed Typhoon Committee? Why will a storm be called Typhoon Dim-sum? Dim-sum was Hong Kong’s contribution to the nine new tropical cyclone names introduced in 2026 to the list in the western North Pacific and the South China Sea. It was part of a “reserve list” of tropical cyclone names with regional characteristics developed by the Hong Kong Observatory with the help of the public in 2023. Dim-sum came fourth, with “milktea” coming out on top of the poll which attracted more than 20,000 votes. What are the usual naming protocols for typhoons? There are 140 names on the list compiled by the Typhoon Committee, formed jointly by the United Nations and the World Meteorological Organization to help Asia Pacific countries prepare for tropical storms. Tropical cyclones are also called hurricanes or typhoons, depending on the region. The names of tropical storms are generally recycled and used again, but new names are introduced to replace those which are retired after a cyclone has caused serious casualties and economic losses. Since 2000, each of the 14 member countries provides 10 names, selected from the local language and culture of the area. The change was introduced to better raise cyclone awareness through use of familiar words – such as animals, plants, historical figures and food – that populations could recognise. The first named storm in 2000 was called “Damrey”, meaning elephant in Cambodian, while the US contributed names of Palauan, Marshallese, and CHamoru (also known as Chamorro) origin. Before then, English names had been used. The practice of naming storms started during the second world war when meteorologists from the US defence force named Pacific ocean storms after their wives and girlfriends. What are the other names for tropical cyclones that have just been approved? Nations whose previous contributions are retired, are responsible for proposing new ones but they have to be endorsed by the Typhoon Committee. They cannot be indecent, carry negative connotations in other languages, or be named after public figures. Dim-sum will be joined by North Korea’s contribution of “Gaeguri” (meaning a frog), “Hoaban” (a typical flower of the north-west mountains of Vietnam), and “Tirou” (Micronesia’s contribution, a respectful way of greeting in Chuukese culture). Japan contributed two new names: “Hebi” meaning snake, and “Tomo” meaning stern, while Cambodia chose “Koki” (a large tree), the Republic of Korea “Narae” (the wing of a bird or an insect), and Thailand “Burapha” (East). In 2005, Hong Kong had two proposed names knocked back. Thailand rejected Hong Kong’s suggestion of “Kapok” (meaning a silk-cotton tree in Hong Kong) because it sounded like a Thai slang word for an intimate part of the male anatomy, while “Tai Chi” was opposed by Japanese officials who said it sounded like a child’s name.

title: Trump again rebukes Jeanine Pirro over reflecting pool ‘vandalism’ case
summary: President attacks ‘terrible mistake’ of US attorney, who said in court filing damage stemmed from botched renovation
body: Donald Trump has doubled down on his criticism of Jeanine Pirro after the US attorney for the District of Columbia publicly challenged his claims that vandals had damaged the recently renovated Lincoln Memorial reflecting pool. “She said there was no vandalism. There was tremendous vandalism,” Trump told NBC News on Thursday. “So, she made a terrible mistake. I don’t understand why she did such a stupid thing.” On Friday, Pirro – a former Fox News host and longtime Trump ally who he handpicked to serve as the top prosecutor for the nation’s capital – moved to dismiss vandalism charges against a former Olympian and three others in connection with incidents at the reflecting pool. In a 20-page court filing, Pirro’s office wrote that the damage to the concrete-bottomed tourist attraction was the result of a “botched” renovation – “not vandalism”. Asked on Thursday whether he would consider replacing Pirro, Trump told NBC: “I think she made a terrible decision. That doesn’t mean change.” The comments came after a reportedly heated Oval Office meeting on Monday with Trump, Pirro, and interior secretary Doug Burgum. According to the New York Times, Pirro accused Burgum of misleading the president about the rushed renovation by a vendor awarded a no-bid contract from the interior department. Later that evening, Trump told reporters he had not “made a determination” yet as to whether Pirro would be ousted. The White House did not immediately reply to a request for comment. Earlier this week, Trump accused Pirro of having “folded like an umbrella” after the justice department dismissed the case against David Hearn, a former Olympic canoeist who faced a felony property destruction charge that carried a potential sentence of up to 10 years in prison and a $1,000 fine for the act of having touched a chunk of the pool’s newly peeled coating. Hearn, 67, pleaded not guilty. In a statement after the charges were dropped, Hearn’s lawyers said the case should never have been brought, and argued that its dismissal “does not erase the abuse of government power in arresting and charging a patriotic American who did nothing wrong”. “The administration owes Mr Hearn an apology,” they said. Hearn is one of seven people who was charged in connection with what Trump claimed were attempts to vandalize the $15m renovation of the reflecting pool that has been plagued by problems the justice department said was “the result of flawed installation by the contractor”. “Frankly, I think she choked,” Trump said from the Oval Office on Monday. An attorney for Hearn has since said that “all options are on table” for legal action. Those include “civil suits, bar referrals for the prosecutors involved, request for sanctions, and reimbursement of attorneys’ fees and expenses,” Hearn’s attorney Steven Levin said on Tuesday.

title: Airline workers reportedly decline to help US agents as Trump migrant crackdown accelerates
summary: Expansion of immigration enforcement at US airports puts employees at odds with agents seeking 2,000 daily arrests
body: A dramatic increase in immigration enforcement at US airports has reportedly placed the airline industry at odds with the Trump administration as workers decline to help federal officials arrest their targets – many of whom have pending applications for visas, asylum or green cards. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) and the Transportation Security Administration (TSA) – both part of the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) – have expanded their collaboration to make as many as three dozen daily arrests at US airports last month, the Wall Street Journal reported. Some of the people who have been taken into federal immigration custody include a former au pair, an asylum seeker with sickle cell anemia who uses a wheelchair, and women who are married to US citizens and in the process of applying for lawful permanent residency, according to the New York Times. “It’s not people with criminal records,” said Ghassan Shamieh, a San Francisco-based immigration lawyer who had four clients detained at airports over 10 days. “You are talking about people with legitimate pending applications.” The latest crackdown represents another policy shift for the DHS, which has generally avoided immigration enforcement at airports so as not to disrupt domestic travel. But with a goal of 2,000 daily immigration arrests, ICE has started detaining people – many of whom have overstayed visas after coming to the US legally and have pending applications for immigration relief – in public places far from security checkpoints, whether at ticket counters or near gates. “This administration is working diligently to ensure that aliens in our country illegally can no longer fly unless it is out of our country to self-deport,” a DHS spokesperson told the New York Times. At one point, in Dallas, a federal agent went so far as to try to board a plane in search of a target. But the Southwest Airlines gate agent reportedly refused to allow the officer to do so without a warrant signed by a judge, and airline employees blocked ICE from seeing a computer screen while passengers were boarding. Southwest told the Wall Street Journal that it follows the law and has protocols “to ensure appropriate legal documentation is presented by law enforcement personnel before any information about customers is shared”. Still, hundreds of immigration arrests have already taken place at airports since the TSA and ICE began cooperating with one another last year. Members of the airline industry met with DHS in July to discuss their discomfort with the policy change. On top of the immigrants being detained, experts have raised concerns that the tense encounters could lead to escalation and unsafe conditions for bystanders or airline employees. “The actions that federal enforcement authorities have taken in our workplaces have raised glaring workplace, safety and legal concerns for flight attendants,” Sara Nelson, international president of the Association of Flight Attendants, wrote in a letter to carriers in March.

title: ICE is now tracking nearly 54,000 immigrants via ankle monitors
summary: Shift in monitoring methods has led to revenue boost for Geo Group, a private prison firm, that also makes the device
body: The US is tracking nearly 54,000 immigrants through GPS-enabled ankle monitors as part of a US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) electronic surveillance program, according to private prison corporation The Geo Group. Early last year, just 17,000 immigrants were wearing the devices.. The Geo Group owns BI Inc, the company that runs ICE’s intensive supervision appearance program (ISAP), and reported the numbers in its earnings call on Thursday. The overall number of immigrants enrolled in the surveillance program remained flat at about 184,000. Geo Group executives said that a large number of participants were shifted from less intensive forms of surveillance, such as phone check-ins, to ankle monitors. The shift to ankle monitors, which the company pitches as a “high-security level of monitoring”, has increased revenues for Geo Group . Ankle monitors cost ICE more than most of the other surveillance technologies administered by BI Inc. The company charges ICE a little more than $2 a day per monitor, while the SmartLink app – a facial recognition and location tracking smart phone app – costs about $0.96 for each immigrant enrolled, according to publicly available ICE statistics. At last count, more than 127,000 immigrants are required to check in using SmartLink. “If this trend continues, the technology and case management mix shift will continue to increase revenues and earnings generated under the ISAP contract even if overall participation counts remain relatively stable,” said George Zoley, Geo Group chairman and CEO, on an earnings call on Thursday. ICE directed agents in June 2025 to move more immigrants enrolled in ISAP to the ankle monitor program, according to a memo obtained by the Washington Post. In a new class action lawsuit filed against ICE in June, immigration advocacy groups allege this “ankle monitors for all” policy “imposes continuous, real-time GPS monitoring without individualized justifications”. Individuals are being subjected to constant surveillance “without meaningful review, explanation, or opportunity to challenge these conditions”, the statement announcing the lawsuit read. That includes pregnant women, who the Guardian first reported were being fitted with smart watches. “ICE has offered no justification for their ‘ankle monitors for all’ policy, but it serves their interest in making daily life harder for immigrants, while also increasing profits for their friends in the private prison industry,” said Evan Benz, managing attorney at the Amica Center for Immigrant Rights, in a statement announcing the lawsuit. The Guardian has reached out to the Department of Homeland Security. Anticipating an increase in reliance on ankle monitors, Geo Group began investing in building out its inventory of the GPS devices at the start of 2025. At the time, the company said it was investing $16m into manufacturing enough ankle monitors to “be in a position to scale up the federal government’s utilization of ISAP by several hundreds of thousands to upwards of several millions of participants as required”. While the company’s predictions of an increase in the use of ankle monitors to track immigrants has started to pan out, investors on Thursday expressed concern about the lack of growth in overall numbers of immigrants being monitored through ISAP. Previously, Geo Group executives said they expected the Trump administration’s immigration agenda would result in a surge in the number of immigrants monitored through ISAP, allowing them to surpass the previous peak of 370,000 under the Biden administration. The company said they thought there would be enough demand from the US government to expand the surveillance program to monitor more than 400,000 immigrants. Without going into specifics, Zoley said he was optimistic that recent shifts in policy could increase the number of people who “would be subject to immigration enforcement … So at a later point, maybe next year, we could see ISAP increase dramatically.” The Trump administration has most recently revoked Temporary Protected Status for Haitians, potentially subjecting hundreds of thousands of people in the US to detention or deportation. Company executives have said in the past that they expect the numbers of immigrants enrolled in ISAP to grow once the government runs out of capacity in detention centers. ISAP was first introduced as an alternative to detention and has been operated by BI Inc since 2004. The program relies on several forms of monitoring in addition to the GPS-ankle monitors, including smart watches that provide real-time location tracking, and a smart phone app. People in the program have reported that the ankle monitors, designed and produced by BI, can overheat, shock them or have been put on too tightly and that there’s little government oversight over the program.

title: US law enforcement gave false information in case against woman charged in anti-ICE protest
summary: Journalist Georgia Fort was one of nearly 40 people charged after interrupting a Minnesota church service
body: Law enforcement officials provided false information to federal judges as they sought to build a criminal case against the independent journalist Georgia Fort in connection with a January protest, her lawyers said in court filings Thursday asking that the charges against her be dismissed. Fort was one of nearly 40 people charged after demonstrators interrupted a service at Cities Church in St Paul, Minnesota after they learned an ICE official was a pastor there. Trump administration officials vowed to arrest anyone involved in the protest. Fort and the former CNN anchor Don Lemon were among those charged with conspiring to interfere with the religious rights of parishioners at their house of worship. They both have strongly denied the charges. In at least 15 applications for search warrants, an investigator with Homeland Security Investigations (HSI) said Fort had been chanting with protesters when they entered the church, her lawyers said. The justice department later conceded the claim was false. The error was insignificant, justice department lawyers later argued, because it ultimately didn’t make it into the indictment that they filed. The errors were among those detailed in three different motions explaining why the criminal case against Fort should be dismissed. The case prosecutors have sought to make against her violates the first amendment, fails to state an actual crime, and is vindictive, her lawyers say. “The government is punishing Fort for entering a church open to the public (after being invited in, no less) to document a protest, and then filming and disseminating that footage,” her lawyers wrote in one of the filings. “All of the evidence in this case points to the government prosecuting Fort precisely because she is a journalist, and in particular because she engaged in that constitutionally sacred work to amplify a message with which the government vehemently disagrees.” In a 24 July hearing, Fort’s lawyers asked Douglas Micko, a magistrate judge overseeing the case, to examine whether prosecutors misled grand jurors about Fort’s conduct when they convinced them to vote to indict her earlier this year. Prosecutors have already disclosed limited information about what was said to the grand jury, but Fort’s lawyers wanted them to share more. “It is clear to me that in this case the government in many respects, candidly, has gone off the rails,” Matthew Ebert, one of Fort’s lawyers, said at the hearing. “If the government is confused and can’t keep its story straight about the evidence in a 39-defendant case and incorrectly and repeatedly lumps my client, a journalist, together incorrectly with the conduct of others who were engaged in a protest, if they can’t keep it straight, all the more reason I’m concerned about what they said to the grand jury,” he added. Micko ordered prosecutors to turn over all grand jury proceedings related to Fort and Michael Beute, another journalist who was arrested. But that was far from the only issue in how officials went about the case, Fort’s lawyers said in court papers. A judge twice rejected an effort by investigators to obtain Fort’s journalistic work product and noted that they didn’t inform the court of the Privacy Protection Act, a law that protects journalists from having to turn over their work to the government. The government also attempted to gain access to her accounts, including subscriber information like names and contact information of subscribers, from social media platforms directly. When a judge rebuffed them, the investigators used an administrative process designed for customs matters to try to get the information, Fort’s lawyers said. The overall prosecution of the protest has been fraught with other mistakes. Officials claimed in a search warrant application that a congregant had broken her arm during the protest, when she had not, Lemon’s lawyers wrote in a filing earlier this year. And prosecutors initially brought charges against a woman who had nothing to do with the protest, but simply had been in the supermarket parking lot when the demonstrators gathered. They dismissed those charges earlier this year. Several prosecutors departed the US attorney’s office in Minnesota when the case was filed, including a top prosecutor who is now working on Lemon’s defense team. Prosecutors have offered to let 29 of those charged plead guilty to a misdemeanor, the New York Times reported. None have accepted. Fort, a longtime local and independent journalist in Minnesota, went live on social media during her arrest, which occurred at her home when her three children were present. She is being prosecuted in the same courts that have credentialed her as media. In addition to her work as a reporter, she is highly involved in the journalism community. “While I do believe the first amendment will stand, I want people to truly understand the impacts of this process,” Fort wrote on social media after the motions were filed. “And when it’s all said and done, I hope no other journalist ever has to choose between protecting themselves and reporting the truth.” The Minneapolis case is one of several the justice department has brought across the US, bringing criminal charges against wide swaths of people who protested immigration enforcement. Earlier this year, prosecutors in Texas secured decades-long prison sentences for a group of nine people for participating in a demonstration outside an ICE facility where a police officer was shot but not killed, even though there was only one protester involved in the shooting. Prosecutors are also pursuing criminal conspiracy charges against 15 people who demonstrated against the Trump administration’s immigration crackdown in Minnesota. Earlier this year, a top justice department official encouraged prosecutors to “go big” and “go loud” when going after protesters, according to the New York Times. The indictment contained several other false claims, Fort’s lawyers said in court documents. For example, prosecutors said Fort conspired with others ahead of the protest, in a parking lot meeting. But Fort’s filing said she left the assembly after three minutes to go wait in her car, and it was only after that organizers shared details of the protest. Lemon’s livestream footage from that meeting shows Fort observing the protesters from the side, her lawyers said. In the hearing, the government said it’s up to a jury to decide whether crimes were committed. “These are not material falsehoods,” prosecutor Neville Hedley said. “They’re accurate statements. They don’t like the characterization of them. That’s an argument for the jury. If the jury doesn’t believe that there was an obstruction taking place … that’s the outcome from the jury. The government loses the case. But again, those are arguments that can be made to a jury.” Text messages filed in court papers by Fort’s lawyers show routine discussions between a reporter and protest organizers, and do not reveal any collaborative planning. The night before, Nekima Levy Armstrong, the lead organizer, messaged Fort. “If we do an action tomorrow morning, available to cover it? We are not doing a press release because it is not a typical protest,” she wrote. “It’s more similar to the #OperationPullUp actions I led after Daunte Wright was killed. Let me know. Thanks”. Fort immediately responded “yup” and said she thought she had been to “every operation pull up action”. The next morning, Fort was running late, and texted Armstrong to say she needed the address of where they were going. Prosecutors also claimed Fort and another man stood outside the church and blocked a van from leaving. Fort was interviewing the protest organizer at the time, and her own livestream shows the van was able to easily leave. “The government has also admitted that it did not begin investigating the case in earnest until after securing the first indictment,” Fort’s attorneys noted in a filing, “despite the justice department’s own policies that require the government to thoroughly assess evidence and discovery obligations before charges are filed, not afterward”. Fort’s lawyers also detailed how the criminal charges against her have deterred her own reporting. She stopped reporting on the protest after she was charged, they said, given the fact that she was a criminal defendant. She had also been covering a boycott against the retailer Target, but stopped doing so after the charges because the two co-founders of the boycott are also defendants. “Fort is also now highly conscious of everything she puts out into the public domain, realizing it could be used against her in this case,” they wrote. “Unlike most other defendants who are not journalists, however, this has a disproportionately heavy impact on Fort’s ability to perform her constitutionally protected work.”

title: Mitch McConnell announces discharge from rehabilitation center
summary: Republican, 84, absent from Senate after fall that led to hospital stay, says he will continue recovery at home
body: The Republican US senator Mitch McConnell has been discharged from a rehabilitation center following the fall that left him hospitalized, he announced on Thursday. McConnell, 84, whose weeks‑long absence from Capitol Hill fueled mounting speculation about his health, said he will continue his recovery at home. While the Senate is set to wrap up legislative business this week, before a five‑week recess, several agenda items remain – including a vote to confirm Todd Blanche as US attorney general. McConnell’s absence further narrows Republicans’ already tight path to approving Donald Trump’s former personal attorney as head of the Department of Justice. McConnell is one of the highest-profile figures in Congress, as a former Senate majority leader. He has been absent from the Senate and not seen in public since mid-June, although his office has released several photos of him. “On the advice of my doctors, I’ll maintain an intensive regimen of physical therapy from home during the state work period,” McConnell said in a Thursday statement. “And I’ll continue to engage with my staff and colleagues on important Senate business.” His 53‑day absence has drawn scrutiny from lawmakers in both parties. Last month, Kentucky’s Democratic governor, Andy Beshear, publicly urged McConnell to release more information about his health, writing: “Kentuckians have grown increasingly concerned about the current state of your health and wellbeing, and ability to hold office.” McConnell was admitted to hospital on 14 June. His office initially offered few details, saying only that he was “continuing to improve”. A month later, McConnell disclosed that a fall at his home and a “mild case of pneumonia” had prompted the hospitalization and his extended time away. In late July, his office said he still had not been cleared to return to work.

title: Aipac-linked Super Pacs spend millions in California to thwart progressive candidate
summary: More than $5m in recent weeks have been spent in ads targeting Aisha Wahab and in support of Melissa Hernandez
body: Super Pacs tied to the American Israel Public Affairs Committee (Aipac) have spent millions in a California congressional race to keep a progressive Democrat from winning Eric Swalwell’s former seat. Aisha Wahab, a state senator who has been endorsed by the California Democratic party, is widely considered the frontrunner in the special election for the district covering a swathe of the East Bay. Swalwell had been in office for more than a decade when he resigned earlier this year following multiple allegations of sexual assault. Wahab outpaced her closest competitor, Melissa Hernandez, the president of the board of directors for the Bay Area Rapid Transit (Bart) agency and a former Dublin mayor, in a June primary as well as a special election to complete the remainder of Swalwell’s term, by more than 20 points. They are set to face off against each other in a runoff election later this month, and then again in November. Super Pacs are pouring money into the race, dropping more than $5m in recent weeks and supporting pro-Hernandez ads and Wahab attack ads, Politico reported on Thursday. The spending includes $1.2m from United Democracy Project, which is backed by Aipac, and $2.1m from Bold America Pac, which has received significant financial backing from the United Democracy Project, according to the outlet. Track Aipac, which tracks the group’s funding of US politicians, reported that the lobby has spent more than $4.4m to support Hernandez in the race. Wahab said there has been a barrage of attack ads against her in the last month that have misrepresented her record, particularly as it relates to public safety issues. She described the Super Pacs’ involvement as election interference. “You have to ask yourself, why? Aipac is clearly not interested in having diverse voices at the table, they are not interested in supporting the Jewish community and a peaceful dialogue,” she argued. “They want a puppet they can control.” The ads have generated outrage among her constituents, she said, adding that her campaign fields calls and emails daily from people “disgusted by the ads”. People are familiar with her record, Wahab added, and her personal history. Her father was murdered when she was a child, and Wahab grew up in the foster care system. As a state lawmaker, she has prioritized victims, she said, and supported legislation to make human trafficking a serious felony and a bill of rights for sexual assault survivors. Aipac, which is one of the largest Super Pacs and the most powerful pro-Israel lobby organization in the US, has significantly expanded its political spending in recent years. The New York Times reported earlier this week that Aipac has doubled its spending, largely in Democratic primaries, to $67.2m. The organization spent millions to support moderate Haley Stevens in Michigan’s Democratic Senate primary. The progressive Abdul El-Sayed ultimately won the primary race in what has been described as a defining contest for the party. Wahab pointed to her record and wide-ranging support, including endorsements from the organization Our Revolution to state and local officials including the attorney general Rob Bonta and the Alameda county sheriff, Yesenia Sanchez. The Guardian has contacted Aipac, and the Hernandez campaign for comment.

title: Iran says a deal with Oman to reopen the strait of Hormuz is close to being finalised – as it happened
summary: This live blog is now closed.
body: Iran said a deal with Oman to reopen the strait of Hormuz is close to being finalised, with reports suggesting Tehran would have control over ships entering the Gulf through the strategic waterway. But despite reports of potentially one of the biggest concessions yet to Iran, Reuters said Iranian sources ⁠rejected Donald Trump’s claims that a deal to reopen the strait was imminent, saying important details were still to be agreed. Iran has made a concerted diplomatic push with Gulf states, warning them explicitly that Tehran will hit their oil, power and water plants unless they convince Trump to end US strikes on Iran and seek a negotiated end to the war, Reuters reports. Sources told Reuters that the message was delivered through a flurry of high-level diplomatic contacts after Trump threatened on 28 July to strike Iran’s energy network and infrastructure. “The Iranian warning was unequivocal: if America targeted Iran’s infrastructure, they would retaliate by striking Gulf energy facilities and other regional targets,” one Gulf source said. Yemeni authorities said on Thursday that they would retaliate to several Houthi rebel attacks earlier in the day, which medical sources told AFP had killed at least 38 government troops and injured 29 in the deadliest toll since the 2022 truce between both sides. The defence ministry of Yemen’s internationally recognised government said in a statement that its armed forces would respond to the missile and drone attacks “at the appropriate place and time”. The Iran-backed Houthis had earlier confirmed that they were behind the attacks on military camps in Yemen that left dozens dead. Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree said the group had deployed ballistic missiles and drones on what they described as Saudi mobilisation in the Al-Ruwyk, Al-Abr, and Al-Thaniyah areas of Yemen. The attacks, he said, were in response to “large Saudi military buildups in their final stages, aimed at escalating the aggression against the liberated provinces”. “We will continue the ‘siege for siege’ equation until the siege on our country is lifted,” Saree added. Meanwhile, Donald Trump insisted that he is “extremely happy” ⁠with the work his defence secretary Pete Hegseth is ⁠doing at ‌the Pentagon, ‌dismissing a ‌report that the two clashed over concerns about US munitions shortages ‌after five months of war against Iran. It comes after the Washington Post (paywall) reported that the US president and Hegseth clashed during a cabinet meeting at Camp David last Friday over the munitions shortages, with Trump reportedly demanding answers after being under the impression the issue “had been fixed”. The shortages were part of the reason that Trump had to call off what he said would be “the biggest attack since World War II” in recent days, sources told the paper. Hegseth reportedly blamed his deputy for the shortages and for Trump not being fully informed on the matter. It came after Trump hit back on Wednesday night at media reports suggesting the US was running low on weapons. The US has “massive amounts of munitions, especially of certain types,” he said in a Truth Social post, adding: “Additionally, large amounts are being manufactured and shipped to the U.S. as needed.” He continued: “Defense companies are building the largest number of plants and factories in our country’s history. The ‘leakers’ of these treasonous statements are being hunted down.” The 7th round of US-mediated talks between Israel and Lebanon in Rome, which concluded on Thursday, were “productive” at the technical and expert levels, according to the US state department. Spokesman Tommy Pigott said in a statement that “Lebanon and Israel are much closer to reaching an agreement on advancing and expanding the pilot zones process”, but did not give further details. There were three days of talks in Rome, the second of which was cut short after Israel resumed heavy strikes on southern Lebanon on Wednesday, accusing Hezbollah of violating the fragile ceasefire agreement initially agreed upon on 26 June. But as the United Nations and local authorities have noted, Israel had continued to launch periodic airstrikes, shelling, and demolitions in the areas of southern Lebanon it’s occupying, despite the truce, killing more than 350 people. The renewed Israeli attacks came as hundreds thousands of displaced people had begun returning to their homes in southern Lebanon, only to be forced to flee again under new orders from the IDF. Two weeks ago, the Lebanese army was allowed to deploy to one of the first “pilot zones”, after Israeli troops pulled out of the village of Zawtar al-Gharbiyeh. Since then, Israel has largely refused to withdraw its troops from the areas it occupies in Lebanon until Hezbollah disarms. More than 4,300 people have been killed since Israel began its attacks and ground invasion of Lebanon, according to the Lebanese health ministry. Over 12,000 have been injured and more than 1.2 million displaced. Iran has made a concerted diplomatic push with Gulf states, warning them explicitly that Tehran will hit their oil, power and water plants unless they convince Donald Trump to end US strikes on Iran and seek a negotiated end to the war, Reuters reports. According to a senior Iranian official, the ‌warning envisaged attacks on the energy facilities, oil fields, refineries, electricity grids, water infrastructure, transport networks and other strategic assets of Washington’s closest Arab allies. The sources told Reuters that the message was delivered through a flurry of high-level diplomatic contacts after Trump threatened on 28 July to strike Iran’s energy network and infrastructure. Iran’s foreign minister, Abbas Araghchi, urged Washington’s ⁠Gulf allies to use their influence with Trump to dissuade him from launching renewed strikes, the senior diplomat said, warning that any attack on Iran would prompt retaliation against US assets and critical infrastructure across the Gulf. His message was consistent in every conversation, the diplomat said: We’re ready to retaliate, but finding a diplomatic solution is the best way to avoid wider escalation and destruction across the region. “The Iranian warning was unequivocal: if America targeted Iran’s infrastructure, they would retaliate by striking Gulf energy facilities and other regional targets,” one Gulf source said. Saudi crown prince Mohammed bin Salman subsequently spoke with Trump, urging him to delay military action, return to negotiations, secure a ceasefire and pursue a diplomatic settlement, the senior diplomat and Gulf sources told Reuters. On 2 August, the US president said he agreed to cancel the attack on Iran “subject to being able to rapidly make a deal”. US Central Command has said it is continuing to enforce the US blockade against Iran, which has been back in place since 14 July as part of Washington’s efforts to pressure Tehran into negotiations. In a post on X on Thursday, Centcom said US marines redirect 49 commercial vessels, disabled two and boarded two other vessels. Yemeni authorities said on Thursday that they would retaliate to several Houthi rebel attacks earlier in the day, which medical sources told AFP had killed at least 38 government troops and injured 29 in the deadliest toll since the 2022 truce between both sides. The defence ministry of Yemen’s internationally recognised government said in a statement that its armed forces would respond to the missile and drone attacks “at the appropriate place and time”. As we reported earlier, the Iran-backed Houthis confirmed that they were behind the attacks on military camps in Yemen that left dozens dead. Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree said the group had deployed ballistic missiles and drones on what they described as Saudi mobilisation in the Al-Ruwyk, Al-Abr, and Al-Thaniyah areas of Yemen. The attacks, he said, were in response to “large Saudi military buildups in their final stages, aimed at escalating the aggression against the liberated provinces”. “We will continue the ‘siege for siege’ equation until the siege on our country is lifted,” Saree added. It comes after the Houthis said on Wednesday that they had attacked two Saudi oil tankers with ballistic missiles, amid the group’s naval blockade of the kingdom. The country’s conflict has become the latest front in the US-Iran war, with Yemen increasingly at risk of being pushed into a more intense cycle of violence and retaliation after the Houthi rebels upended a 2022 truce with the Saudi-backed government last month. Trump posted on his Truth Social platform on Thursday: The Fake News, as usual, is spreading false and completely unfounded rumors. I am extremely happy with the job that Pete Hegseth is doing. Everything has been extraordinary, including our attack on Venezuela, where the result was accomplished in less than one day, allowing us to bring one of the worst criminals anywhere in the World, Nicolas Maduro, to Justice! Likewise, Iran, where the country has been decimated for the purpose of NOT ALLOWING IT TO EVER HAVE A NUCLEAR WEAPON, is going very well! Pete is highly respected within the Military, and has made tremendous improvements, including getting rid of DEI, and increasing recruitment to historic levels. This rumor was started by The Washington ComPost, one of the worst Media Outlets in the business, despite our telling them their story is completely FALSE. title: Trump administration to pay German firm $1.22bn to cut offshore wind leases
summary: Agreement with RWE is fifth deal Trump team has made with energy companies, offering payouts to give up projects
body: The German energy company RWE has reached a $1.22bn deal with the US government to relinquish its offshore wind leases and instead redirect funds towards fossil fuel investments. The agreement marks the fifth deal the Donald Trump administration has struck with energy companies, offering payouts in exchange for abandoning renewable energy projects and redirecting investment towards fossil fuels. This latest deal takes it to almost $4bn of taxpayer money spent on killing offshore wind projects. Announcing the deal with the US interior department on Thursday, RWE said it had agreed to give up its offshore wind leases off the coasts of New York, California and Louisiana. “After careful consideration, it was determined there is no path forward to permit these projects in the US for the foreseeable future,” the company said, referring to the leases it initially secured with a “long-term commitment to develop offshore wind capacity”. RWE paid $1.1bn for its New York lease in a 2022 auction held by the Joe Biden administration, while its leases in Louisiana and California cost a combined $163m, Reuters reports. “The settlement resolves RWE US Offshore’s legal claims and provides $1.22 billion in settlement funds,” RWE continued, adding that the deal would allow it to “direct resources toward energy projects that can be advanced with certainty.” As part of the agreement, RWE will spend $900m to acquire a 16% stake in an unnamed Louisiana liquified natural gas (LNG) project. The company said the settlement proceeds would be used to fund construction of the terminal. RWE has also signed a $300m turbine reservation agreement under which it will develop a pipeline of 15 natural gas peaker plants across the country. The interior secretary, Doug Burgum, hailed the deal, saying on Thursday: “We welcome RWE’s agreement and voluntary investment in projects that strengthen our nation’s energy security, provide dependable baseload power, and help keep electricity affordable for hardworking Americans today while supporting our country’s long-term energy future.” The RWE agreement appears to be the largest deal the Trump administration has struck with an energy company to kill clean energy projects. Earlier agreements with other companies, including TotalEnergies and Duke Energy, amounted to $2.7bn in taxpayer money. Following the Trump administration’s $928m deal with French energy company TotalEnergies to cancel its offshore wind lease off the coast of New York, seven states, including New York, sued the administration over what the New York attorney general, Letitia James, described as a “sham deal” and “illegal agreement”. The administration has also spent up to $1.1bn to boost coal, a move critics argue is “fattening the wallets of his cronies” while raising working Americans’ energy bills, particularly as the US’s war on Iran drives up fuel prices. At the same time, the federal government is seeking to slash public input periods for fossil fuel drilling on federal lands while shifting more of the financial risks of cleanup to taxpayers. Meanwhile, a report released last fall by the Environmental Integrity Project found that every fully operational LNG facility in the US had violated federal pollution limits in recent years. According to the non-profit research organization, violations included the discharge of illegal amounts of bacteria, zinc, oil and other pollutants into waterways, as well as failures of terminal managers to submit monitoring reports for waterway discharge.

title: TikTok creator Sydney Towle, who shared cancer journey, dies aged 26
summary: The creator documented her battle with rare bile duct cancer, inspiring more than a million followers online
body: Sydney Towle, a TikTok creator who shared her battle with stage 4 cholangiocarcinoma, or bile duct cancer, with over a million online followers, has died at age 26, her family announced on Thursday. Towle gained fame for her posts about her life as a spirited young woman who encouraged her TikTok followers to rethink how a cancer patient might look and live. Towle’s family announced her death, nearly three years after she was first diagnosed, via Instagram: “We will always love you so much Sydney,” the caption read. “I am so proud of how hard you fought. I love you.” Earlier this week, her family said that she had entered hospice care. In 2023, Towle was living in Los Angeles after graduating from Dartmouth College, and working at a remote-office marketing job, surfing and posting bikini selfies and dance trend videos online. A bulge and burning sensation in her abdomen landed her in urgent care and she later was diagnosed with cholangiocarcinoma, a rare cancer most often diagnosed in adults over age 50. “The doctor thought I had a hernia, but he was like, ‘I’ll send you in for an ultrasound, just in case,’” Towle told Today in 2024. “I got an ultrasound, and it showed a solid mass.” Towle turned her medical ordeal as a young woman with cancer into content, creating videos of a hike in Spain during a solo adventure in Europe, her mom wrapping her head in ice packs to help combat hair loss from cancer treatments, and the day-to-day of her struggle balanced with gratitude and hope. She blended her life as a cancer patient with lifestyle posts and faced online trolls who doubted the reality of her condition and online persona. “I’m not a television show that you’re watching, which I think people have a really hard time understanding,” she told the New York Times in a 2025 front-page profile. “I’m not a fake character. I’m a person.” In a TikTok posted last year Towle danced in her apartment advising her fans: “Go get a pint of Ben and Jerry’s, watch your favorite movie, remember that life is good and bad things happen sometimes but that doesn’t make it a bad life.” Melinda Bachini, of the Cholangiocarcinoma Foundation, told the Times that Towle’s role as an influencer had persuaded her audience to reconsider living with a serious illness. “Syd had a keen sense of how sharing her life could help others, and she used that to promote understanding of young adults facing cancer, the importance of research funding and the beauty of living life in the moment,” she said. After her death was announced on Thursday, her mother and brother Austin Towle’s TikTok video update was flooded with messages of condolence.

title: Trump denies US low on key munitions in war with Iran after reports of shortages
summary: President’s comment come after report he had demanded answers from Pete Hegseth over alleged shortages
body: Donald Trump has lashed out at reports that the US is running short of key munitions in its war with Iran, threatening long prison sentences for officials who leak information about the military’s weapons stocks. The US president claimed on Thursday that the US had “massive amounts” of ammunition and said more was being manufactured and shipped to the region, as his frustration over the conflict spilled into a public attack on the media. “Defense companies are building the largest number of plants and factories in our country’s history,” Trump wrote on his Truth Social platform, without providing evidence or details about the specific weapons in question. His remarks came after a report that he had demanded answers from his defense secretary, Pete Hegseth, over alleged shortages at a cabinet meeting last Friday at Camp David, the US presidential retreat in Maryland. Trump told Hegseth he felt misled because he believed the problem “had been fixed”, according to the Washington Post newspaper, citing two unnamed sources familiar with the exchange. Hegseth defended himself and sought to shift blame to his deputy, Stephen Feinberg, the Post reported. The president responded angrily on Thursday, accusing the media of spreading “treasonous statements” and warning that those responsible would be pursued. “The ‘leakers’ of these treasonous statements are being hunted down,” he wrote. “Long term jail sentences will be sought!” CNN separately reported that shortages of long-range guided missiles and air defence interceptors had begun to constrain Trump’s strategy in the conflict. The US military had “nearly exhausted 80%” of its stock of Terminal High Altitude Area Defense (Thaad) interceptors, the network said. The Washington Post also reported that concerns over dwindling supplies had contributed to Trump calling off further strikes against Iran, despite his repeated threats to hit the Islamic Republic “very hard”. The White House and Pentagon rejected the claims. Karoline Leavitt, the White House press secretary, described the account of the Camp David exchange as “FAKE NEWS!” on X. She wrote: “I was at Camp David with President Trump and Secretary Hegseth. This literally never happened.” Seeking to quash speculation about Hegseth’s future, Leavitt insisted that “the President loves the Secretary and thinks he’s doing a tremendous job”. Sean Parnell, the chief Pentagon spokesperson, dismissed both the reports of a confrontation between Trump and Hegseth and claims of weapons shortages as “equally fictional”. Parnell added: “Secretary Hegseth isn’t going anywhere and he’s going to continue to work side by side with Deputy Secretary Feinberg to execute President Trump’s agenda, strengthen America’s defense industrial base, and ensure our warfighters have every capability they need to deter and defeat any adversary.” Trump himself weighed in later on Thursday. “I am extremely happy with the job that Pete Hegseth is doing,” the president said on social media, accusing outlets reporting otherwise of “spreading false and completely unfounded rumors”. The increasingly public dispute comes as Trump seeks to project confidence over the course of the war. On Sunday he claimed he had ordered and subsequently called off “the biggest attack since” the second world war, in the light of fresh negotiations over the strait of Hormuz. Iran’s foreign ministry denied that talks were taking place, despite Trump’s claim that Tehran was eager to reach a deal. The Pentagon has faced criticism for manipulating US casualty figures and failing to hold regular press briefings about the war. Hegseth, a former Fox News host who styles himself as the secretary of war, last month announced a screening programme for “testosterone deficiency” among US troops. Joe Scarborough, an MS Now host and former Republican congressman, posted on X: “When Hegseth attacks media questions on this extreme munitions shortage as ‘fake news’, he makes this unforgivable blunder worse. Congress needs to take action. Americans need the truth. Hegseth can’t give it. He needs to go.”

title: US federal judge halts order for Trump to turn over financial records to BBC
summary: Judge issues temporary pause while he considers Trump’s request to revise his libel lawsuit against BBC
body: A federal judge has temporarily halted an order requiring Donald Trump to turn over detailed financial information about his business empire to the BBC as part of an ongoing libel lawsuit. US district judge Roy Altman issued the temporary pause while he considers Trump’s request to revise and narrow parts of his lawsuit against the BBC over a 2024 documentary that aired in the UK. Trump’s legal team sought to stop the discovery order that would have given the BBC access to the president’s financial records in the multibillion-dollar case. Trump has argued the BBC’s 2024 documentary about the January 6 attack harmed his business interests. Last month, a Miami-based judge ruled that Trump would have to begin producing extensive financial records by 6 August, including information covering the hundreds of businesses held by the Trump family trust. On Wednesday, Trump’s attorneys asked the court to temporarily suspend that order, arguing the BBC had demanded a “shockingly broad amount of information based on clearly political motivations”. In a four-page order signed on Wednesday and released on Thursday, Altman said Trump’s effort to remove his claims that the documentary damaged his brand and businesses could reduce the BBC’s need to obtain his financial records. Trump’s lawyers are seeking to narrow the claim to alleged reputational harm. The BBC has argued that Trump’s business value remains relevant because his public reputation was closely linked to his success as a businessman. The broadcaster’s lawyers also pointed out that Trump’s proposed amended complaint, which has not yet been made public, still seeks $10bn in damages. They contend that amount would be difficult to support if the case was based only on reputational harm. At the center of the lawsuit is a scene from the BBC documentary Trump: A Second Chance, which edited together portions of Trump’s 6 January 2021 speech in a way that made it appear he directly encouraged supporters to attack the US Capitol. The BBC has apologized for the edit but maintains the defamation allegations lack merit. The lawsuit is part of a series of legal actions Trump has launched against media organizations over coverage he says is defamatory or unfair. In a separate case, Trump’s attorneys argued that his $10bn defamation lawsuit against the Wall Street Journal should proceed to trial after the newspaper reported on a “bawdy” letter the president was said to have contributed to a birthday book for Jeffrey Epstein in 2003. Trump’s justice department also issued subpoenas to New York Times journalists following the newspaper’s reporting on security concerns involving the Air Force One presidential aircraft before later withdrawing those subpoenas.
